pages.name: Overview
pages.html:
A dozen dead, and someone powerful is hiding their names. I want to know who gave that order, and what he is so afraid we will read.
 {{                  Constance Sharp, The Lantern }}

Familiar Hunting Grounds

Dr. Pemberton's shadow is getting stronger, and bolder. It escalates, killing four more in the space of a week, including Father Penance and Claude Skohle. At first the Clarion Society is unresponsive, but when Agent Wakes' surgeon is killed, an official inquiry will begin.

Episode Summary
Players 3–6, Level 6
Duration ~4 hours
Pacing Player-Led Investigation; Chase; Combat
Scenes 6 (4)
Cast Miss Sharp; Sir Stowe; the Special Police; five horrors
Reward A page of the Pale Journals; the Shadow's Journal; jars of stolen memory
References Doom Counter; Dread Insight; Chase System; Curse System; Mythos stat blocks; residential maps

Timeline

Fifteen years ago. A collector had the Pale Journals stolen from the Temple of Anhur in Sai Abbadon.

Two years ago. Zeshagu warriors stormed from the mountains, joined Sous Terreborgue, and took Sai Abbadon.

One year ago. Zeshagu's dragons and Sous Terreborgue's warships seal Anchester; only blockade-runners slip through. The collector has the Journals copied, and pages leak out.

Four and a half months ago. Dr. Aldous Pemberton attends a page-reading on Lantern Avenue. He is changed, and his shadow begins to hunt.

Two and a half months ago. Bodies surface in the lower wards, skulls opened above the brow. The Watch names no suspect; the wards name him the Smiling Man.

Seven weeks ago. Mr. Claude Skohle holds a private reading of a page from the Pale Journals. The Smiling Man kills Dr. Hollow.

Six weeks ago. Dr. Leopold Haeint is found dead with his wife and child, in possession of a Sai Abbadonian mummy and a page from the Pale Journals. The Special Police and the Clarion Society both open inquiries.

These six weeks. The killings quicken. Dr. Thurston Frane, Madame Vellora Sigh, Father Mercer Penance, and Mr. Claude Skohle all fall.

Today. The players decide what to do with what they know.

Episode Structure

This episode branches twice and converges. It opens on one shared scene, forks at Scene 2, forks again at Scene 3, and every path ends at the Finale — so any given party plays four of the six scenes, never all six.

Scene 1 — The Accounting, in which the players account for six weeks of killings and are pushed toward one of two witnesses.

Scene 2, the witness fork (play one): - 2a — The Witness, in which Sharp, found alive, points them at the proof and the men burying it. - 2b — Too Late, in which Wakes is found already taken, and points to the remaining living Skohle House attendees.

Scene 3, the action fork (either witness leads to either): - 3a — The Morgue, in which they breach the North Harbor morgue for a body and a name: a doctor. - 3b — The Debt, in which they race to keep Sir Reginald Stowe alive.

Finale — The Empty House, in which every road ends at Pemberton's door, and the thing he left rises wearing the faces of the dead.

I have seen the wounds. I am no credulous man, yet I can no longer call the hand that made them human.
                    V.C. Lenore, Torch & Clarion

pages.name: The Doom Counter
pages.html:
Start: equal to the party's number of Dread Insights.

Escalating Doom

Mark Escalation
3 Shadow notices the party; call a Mythos check.
6 Shadow stalks; darkness turns hostile. Manifesting Doom costs −1.
9 Shadow strikes a PC, or takes an NPC.
12 Fully hunted; dread rides every scene until Doom falls.

Manifesting Doom

Cost Doom
1 Mythos Disadvantage
1 Murphy's Law
1 You Heard That, Right?
2 Nobody Here but Us Shadows
2 Everyone's a Suspect
2 Cut Off
3 Reset Mythos Monster Abilities
3 Enemy Reinforcements
5 Activate one Dread Ability

CARNIVAL OF
WANDERING WONDERS
Gates open at dusk; children half off.

Doom

Mythos Disadvantage. Impose disadvantage on a single roll, framed as the Mythos pressing in: the hand shakes, the eye slips, the mind stalls.

Murphy's Law. Something mundane fails at the worst moment. A lamp dies, a lockpick snaps, a motorcar won't turn over, a page tears. Cost a resource or a plan, not health.

You Heard That, Right? A sound with no source: a footstep, a wet drag, a laugh in an empty room. Trigger one of the character's Dread Insights.

Nobody Here but Us Shadows. The light fails and the dark takes the scene. Vision drops, the shadow's reach grows, and whatever waits in the black gets bolder.

Everyone's a Suspect. The Special Police turn on the party: a tail, a checkpoint, a search, an accusation. Progress stalls until they talk, run, or pay to shake it.

Cut Off. The way out closes: a door bars, a stair gives way, a crowd surges in. The party is stuck where they stand and must deal with the scene, not flee it.

Reset Mythos Monster Abilities. Refresh a creature's recharge counters and spent abilities. The thing they thought they'd worn down comes back whole.

Enemy Reinforcements. Fresh enemies arrive mid-scene: more shadows, more Special Police, more of whatever they're already facing.

Activate one Dread Ability. Trigger one of a boss creature's Dread Abilities. The priciest spend, for the worst single moment.

pages.name: Scene: The Accounting
pages.html:
Theater of the Mind, ~30 - 45 min

Six weeks have passed since the Haeint House. The Special Police have gone quiet, the war grinds on, and the characters have been left to their own lives in a city that is quietly bleeding. The Accounting is where the table catches up: each player tells the DM what their character did with those six weeks, and the DM answers each stretch of downtime in kind.

It is a scene made of newspapers. As the players account for their time, the DM feeds them the city one piece at a time — a fire down in North Harbor, a shortage on Astor Street, and, set in small type beneath it, the name of someone they knew, dead. The killings mount, faster as the weeks close, until the news stops being background and becomes the thing they cannot look away from.

By the end, two people they care about are still drawing breath: a reporter and a wounded major. Whatever the party chooses to chase points them toward one or the other, and the hunt for the Smiling Man begins in earnest.

pages.name: Scene: The Accounting: Running the Accounting
pages.html:
Running the Accounting

Go round the table. Each character says how they spent the six weeks, and the DM answers each with a consequence. A handout, a broadsheet, a rumor. Feel free to use any that are provided, or make up your own.

After each character interaction, they should have a hook either for the Scene with Ms. Sharp or Col. Wakes.

pages.name: Scene: The Accounting: Possible Leads
pages.html:
Possible Leads

What follows are common leads the players decide what to chase; what follows is only where we expect them to look. If they go somewhere unexpected, answer it the same way.

The Osgoods. A character with family ties may decide to reach out to one of their contacts. A friendly fence, Verrick Hans, has useful knowledge.

The Garrison. A character with old service ties may look up who's left. Colour-Sergeant Bram Tolliver tends the officers' club bar and hears everything worth hearing.

The Almshouse. A character moved by the killings may visit the Church of the Martyr's soup kitchen and talk to Brother Cobbe.

The Carnival. A character drawn to the Tower may pass an evening among the Carnival's wonders. Its troupe carries every rumor in the city and a famed mystic.

The Watch. A character who trusts the law, or who drinks at the Devil's Due, may fall in with Constable Dob Larkin, who says far too much after a few.

The Sanitorium. A character chasing the doctors may present themselves at the Sanitorium gate. They get no further than the yard where the patients wander and murmer to themselves.

Skohle's House. A character who attended the reading may return to the antiquarian's house. It has not been cleared out, and its doors are poorly watched.

Father Mercer Penance Was murdered recently. A handout is provided.

Miss Constance Sharp People the players talk to will have seen here, but do not know where she is presently.

Madame Vellora Sigh Was murdered recently. A handout is provided.

Claude Skohle Was murdered recently. Refer to Skohle's House.

Sir Reginald Stowe People the players talk to will not have seen him in weeks.

Major Lyle Wakes Is recouperating in ICU. The Special Police prevent any attempt to talk to him directly.

Shopping Characters who are looking for rare or interesting things will know of a Fence named Verrick Hans.

The Osgoods

Setting. "The Storehouse" is a cramped supper-house in the back streets of Brasshold. Steam-fogged windows, mismatched tables, the smell of fried onions and gun-oil. The front room feeds dockhands and bruisers; the real business happens in a curtained back booth under a flickering Innovation-lamp that browns out every time the trams pass. Everyone who eats here belongs to somebody.

Verrik Hans is a fence who moves stolen goods and stolen secrets with equal ease. Soft-spoken, watchful, and quick to smile he knows a death before the papers do, often because he fences the dead man's property.

Rumors Hans has heard that there is a journalist asking questions about a hit that was ordered by Madam Merewyn. Rumor has it she's in the wind.

Store Hans has a store of common and uncommon consumable magic items. Scrolls, potions, charms.

The handout. Laying among some papers laid down on the counter, the players see an obituary of the famed actress, Madame Vellora Sigh, dead under mysterious circumstances. Byline: Constance Sharp.

The Garrison

Setting. "The Ravelin" is a convalescent club for wounded officers, a grand hotel gone to seed in the garrison quarter. Gaslight through pipe-smoke, medals pinned to threadbare men, a piano nobody plays, and the blockade guns rattling the glassware. The Innovation-tech radiators clank and bleed steam into the cold.

Colour-Sergeant Bram Tolliver tends the bar, a one-legged veteran who knows every man's business for the price of a drink and an ear. Blunt, kind, and bone-tired.

Rumors Tolliver says the brass are sitting on a surgeon's death, one Frane, who had been tending "the Major, Wakes, up at the hospital." Lower talk has doctors combed from the wards and shipped to the front.

Infirmary The club keeps a surgery below stairs, offering officers and their guests hospital care per the healing matrix.

The handout. A page of "The Garrison" listing the death of Surgeon-Mamor Frame, calling the death sudden and unexplained, and noting the officers he oversaw, "among them Major L. Wakes."

The Almshouse

Setting. "The Martyr's Table" is a soup kitchen and almshouse in the poorest quarter, kept by the Church of the Martyr. Trestle tables, a copper of thin stew, ragged children and old soldiers in the ladle line, a plaster Martyr on the wall with a candle guttering beneath it. Black crepe hangs over the door today, and half the room is red-eyed, a wake that cannot afford to close.

Brother Cobbe is a stooped lay brother who has ladled soup here thirty years and knows every child by name. Gentle, grief-stricken, and talkative in his sorrow, if a character came up on these streets he fed them once and remembers.

VISIT YOUR LOCAL PARISH
 Light a candle, share a burden. The Martyr keeps a place for you.

Rumors. Cobbe grieves that Father Penance is dead, found in his own bolted vestry with his head opened and not a blade nor a drop of blood to say how. Beyond his account, the Table is where the whole poor quarter comes to eat, and the street-children hear everything. Roll or choose:

d12 Overheard at the Table
1 Newspaper lady paying children to watch the North Harbor police-house
2 Major at the rest-hospital won't stop screaming
3 Driver offering money for word of a missing Sir Stowe
4 Men in good coats took the Father's papers, not the regular police
5 Madhouse doctor weeps as he works
6 Killings only on nights the lamps go dark
7 Child saw a shadow stand up and walk off
8 Only clever folk dying
9 Dead found with heads opened, nothing taken
10 Old soldier blames wartime spies
11 Body-snatchers selling heads to the school
12 Father owed the Osgoods

The handout. Laid among the parish notices by the door, the players see a careful obituary praising Father Penance's charitable works and calling the passing sudden and natural. Byline: Constance Sharp.

The Carnival

Setting. The night-fair moored at the Tower, come down from wildspace. Loud, crowded, porous; ask anyone and learn almost anything. Isra's home and found-family.

The Baron owns the Carnival and its debts. Charming out front, colder behind. Talks for a price or a favor of his own.

Work the crowd. Each hand gives one thread:

Ask What you learn
Nab Collyer (gate) Killings only on dark-lamp nights.
Dorca Skein (wardrobe) Victims all came asking after forbidden books and old lore.
Cinder Twins The doctor won't be home.
Bexley (beasts) His animals panic on killing nights.
Xil (wildspace) A shadow that eats knowing, and it serves a master.

Mother Sixpence's prophecy (hand out across the campaign, not all at once): - "The smiling one is no man. He is a man's shadow, and goes home to his master at cockcrow." - "You'll chase him to a doctor's door and find it open and empty." - "When the papers forget him, fear him most. He's followed the guns to the mud." - "The answer sleeps behind the walls where they keep the mad." - "Behind his little grin waits a wider one, patient, that means never to die."

The handout. Same Broadsheet as "The Osgoods", an obituary of the famed actress, Madame Vellora Sigh, dead under mysterious circumstances. Byline: Constance Sharp.

The Watch

Setting. "The Kettle & Truncheon," a low pub a stone's throw from the station house, thick with off-duty constables, pipe smoke, and grievances. One corner where a certain beat copper holds court once he's three pints deep.

Constable Dob Larkin walks a real beat and has read the reports. Weak-willed and sore about it, after a few he turns into "Bellows" and cannot shut up. Tonight he's angry enough to talk.

What Larkin spills. He reels off "the queer ones" and hands the party the whole pattern. "All of them were at that Skohle death house."" Father Penance, found murdered bolted in his vestry; Madame Sigh, locked room; Claude Skohle, behind a metal door in his basement; and Surgeon-Major Frane, in his study at the Garrison. Every one "opened up neat as an egg, not a tool in sight."

He will also talk about the cover-up. How the Special Police took the files and told the station to shut its mouth. That is why Larkin is talking. And it's not that "he won't tell that newspaper woman what he knows", but that he's waiting to see if she'll pay him for it.

No handout.

JOIN THE CITY CONSTABULARY

Anchester wants men and women

of steady nerve to keep the peace.

Walk a beat. Guard the lamps.

Fair wage, uniform, and pension.

So the city may sleep, some must not.

The Sanitorium

Setting. A grim pile behind a high wall. At the desk a starched matron takes your names and turns you out: no visits, no records, no doctors. But the front yard is open, milder patients wandering the gravel and dead flowerbeds under a bored orderly. That is where you get something.

Aunt Winnie (Miss Winifred Sharp) drifts up mid-conversation as though she has known you for years. Gentle, birdlike, cardigan buttoned wrong. Sharp's aunt, committed here, and a patient of the very doctor you are hunting.

Rumors - Her doctor is "the one who cries all the time, poor thing, always weeping," and his dark raincoat, "you know the kind, the sort that stands in the corner waiting to give you a hug." - So sad about Mrs. Sigh. She remembers her playing Yoricina in Small Town Murders, and wasn't her voice just angelic. - She does hope her niece visits soon. "She's a big-time reporter, you know. She wrote this."

The handout. Same Broadsheet as "The Osgoods", an obituary of the famed actress, Madame Vellora Sigh, dead under mysterious circumstances. Byline: Constance Sharp.

Skohle's House

Setting. Claude Skohle's antiquarian townhouse, the same rooms where the players sat for the page-reading in The Edge of Darkness, now cold and curtained. Down in the basement, behind a metal strongroom door still bolted from within, Skohle lies dead at last, his skull opened along the seams with no blade and no cause. After weeks of reading it in the papers, they stand where it happened and see the Smiling Man's work for themselves; nothing but a shadow could have passed that door. The Special Police came and went in a hurry, took papers and not curios, and left the house much as it was, its doors poorly watched.

The reward. The strongroom is why they came back. Skohle's collection is still here, the curios, rare volumes, and hidden cache they could not grab that first night, at least one genuinely useful one-use item, and his private research.

The letters. A bundle on the writing desk in his study, sealed letters to that night's guests (Penance, Sigh, Wakes, Sharp, Stowe) and personal letters to each PC who attended the reading. Skohle was tying up his affairs and passing along a fear. The PC letters are bespoke GM hooks; the letters to Wakes and Sharp each point the party on toward a living witness.

pages.name: SCENE: DANGEROUS DAME
pages.html:
Garden of Lights. Night. ~60 minutes.

Over the past six weeks, the players have been pounding the streets trying to figure out what is going on. They have uncovered clues that lead them to search for Miss Constance Sharp, of The Lantern. While she has been covering her tracks, word has gotten back to her that several men and woman of sound credentials are looking for her. She is acquainted with a few of them.

She will send word for the players to meet her at the Garden of Lights in Kingsgreen.

A thousand gas globes burn the Garden of Lights bright as a summer noon, the boldest blaze in a city that puts out its lamps and prays. The only people out under it are the young, the drunk, and the brave, lovers and revelers who would rather be seen than sit home in the dark, and they laugh a little too loud. Far beyond the walls the skytower's beam and the long searchlights rake slow across the black, hunting a sky that has not come this deep into the city. Not yet.

The Garden burns this bright on purpose, and that purpose is the whole scene. It is the one place in the city the Smiling Man cannot follow, because there is no shadow in it to hunt from. That is why Sharp chose it, and why it stands out under the searchlights like a struck match. Everything turns on one line the party must not be pushed across: the gates. Driven out of the light into the dark streets is worse than anything the Special Police can do inside. The only way out that is not the dark is the Clarion motor, the Tea Kettle, idling at the north gate.

Miss Sharp

She has been watching the gates since before the party arrived, and will not approach until she is satisfied they came alone. She makes contact through a cut-out: a flower-seller with a bloom and a bench number, a boy with a folded card, a waiter who seats them at a table she chose.

Play her disturbed, not deranged. She has a page of the Pale Journals in her bag, and she has read it. She does not sleep. She checks her reflection in every dark pane. She loses the thread of a sentence and catches it a beat later, and hates that it shows. Under all of it she is still the sharpest person in the Garden, frightened in a way she cannot file under any heading she trusts. She leads with the character she knows, and everything follows from that trust.

What she hands over across the meeting:

  • The reframe. "You've been reading it as a murder. It isn't. It's a robbery. Somebody is stealing what these people knew, right out of their heads, and somebody with a warrant is making very sure nobody writes it down."
  • The pattern. Every one of the dead read a page, or went hunting the old lore. Every one was found with the skull opened along the seams, no blade, no way in. One hand. Only the clever ones.
  • The cover-up. The Special Police took every file, every photograph, every coroner's note, and told the Watch to forget the business.
  • The proof, and the ask. How these people truly died, a body and the coroner's own notes with the consulting doctor's name on them, sits in the North Harbor morgue, the one place the Special Police could not scrub. She cannot get in alone. This is the road to the Gravedigger scene.
  • The page. She has one, and reading it is taking something out of her by inches. She will not say what she saw.

When the Police Close In

They have been drifting into the Garden at its edges the whole meeting, unhurried, in good coats. Sharp spots them first, because she has been looking all night, and stops mid-sentence, her eyes going flat and steady on something past the party's shoulders.

If the party reaches for weapons, she is appalled: "Are you mad? You can't fight the Special Police, there's no end of them, and by morning there'll be a bill with your faces on it. Put it away." When the first coat closes, she is done arguing: "Don't shoot. Don't you dare. Run."

The exits are the wheel of avenues. Go to the chase.

Running the Chase

The party runs as one token, Sharp riding with it, pace set by the group. They start at Step 3. The Special Police pursue from Step 0. Reaching Step 10 is reaching the Tea Kettle at the north gate. Each turn the party moves a step and may push for more; a failed push or a placed event triggers a complication. If the Police ever share the party's step, they close: resolve as combat, or as a grab for Sharp or the page.

Every complication is a situation, not an order. The players choose how they meet it, a clean answer buys distance and a poor one costs it. The party may fight a rearguard, split off a decoy, or scoop up and carry Sharp at any time; adjudicate those as a move, not a roll.

Place three of these as fixed events on the track before you start, and roll the rest. Recommended fixed placements: the Lamp-Tree, the Reflecting Pond, the Cordon.

Conclusion

At Step 10 the party reaches the Tea Kettle and steams into the dark streets, the Garden shrinking behind into a single island of light. Sharp lights a cigarette with a hand that will not quite hold still and does not pretend otherwise. Rook hands the players a ticker tape that the Teakettle spit out right before they got into the vehicle.

The players have a choice, they can help Sharp break into the North Harbor Watch Station in Gravedigger, or chase down the souce of the cryptic message in Stowe Away

pages.name: Scene:Wake for Major Wake
pages.html:
Hostpital. Day. ~45 minutes.

The party took the Wakes road and arrived too late. Major Lyle Wakes, the wounded Clarion man from the Edge of Darkness reading, was held under Special Police guard in the secure ward. Empty post, cold room, and in a hospital that never sleeps, no alarm.

The ward runs on around you, trolleys and low voices and somebody's radio two rooms down. Only the door at the end is wrong. Two chairs sit empty where two men should be standing, and past them the secure room lies open: the bed dented and thrown back, the straps hanging loose, and a supper tray on the side table crawling with maggots. Nurses cross the corridor behind you without a glance at any of it.

Missing

Skill challenge, DC 12, three successes before three failures. Any approach, and keep it generous. Every thread leads to the stairwell at the end of the hall. Three successes, they descend forewarned; three failures, they descend cold and what waits gets the drop.

What Lies Below

The stairs let you out into the cold store beneath the wards, low and dark and ticking with pipes, the smell of chemicals laid over something spoiled. Two shapes crouch in the dark, grey and hunched, worrying at something on the floor. They were your guards an hour ago. Between them a third man stands very still in hospital whites. It is Major Wakes, and he turns to face you, and he is smiling, and the smile is not his.

They came to save him; he greets them with his own face. If a PC knew Wakes, land the turn on them.

The fight. Two ghouls (the guards), one Mythos Ghast (Wakes); stat blocks in the bestiary. Opener set by the search: forewarned, the party goes first with advantage; cold, the things below take a surprise round. Ghouls swarm, the Ghast is the threat. Mythos encounter: land the scripted Insight (Wis save, lowest fails) and tick Doom.

In his fist. The Lantern Society page on Lady Ridgely's hat, Sir Reginald Stowe's name ringed hard, over and over, nearly through the paper.

Conclusion

The players have made it out of the hospital alive with a little more information than they had when they entered. A broadsheet with Sir Reginald Stowe's name circled over and over, and if the players notice, Constance Sharp's by-line on the Obituary about Madame Sigh.

As they settle into the teakettle, Rook hands the players a ticker tape that the Teakettle spit out right before they got into the vehicle.

As the Teakettle begins to putter away, Rook slams on the breaks. The door opens and Constance Sharp gets in. She will quickly tell them her plan to break into the North Harbor Watch Station and find the name of the Doctor who she is certain is the killer.

The players have two choices. They can follow Sharp to Gravedigger, or chase down Stowe in Stowe Away.

pages.name: SCENE: Gravedigger
pages.html:
North Harbor Morgue. Night. ~45 minutes.

Sharp's key lets the party into the morgue in the HQ basement, the room they never reached in Dance of Death. They came for the autopsy records and the name of the doctor who signed them.

The stair down is colder with every step, and the smell finds you before the room does, carbolic and old meat. The morgue is a long vault of steel drawers and porcelain slabs under low electric light. At the far slab a small round man in a rubber apron is busy with something you cannot quite see, humming a hymn a half-tone flat. He does not turn around. "With you presently," he says. "They are ever so patient down here."

Something Behind His Eyes

The undertaker is Mr. Betterton, and the Fluke has ridden him for days. He is courteous, damp-eyed, and wrong, and he tends the dead the way no mortician would, rearranging them, talking to them, feeding. He will stall and smile as long as the party stays polite. The moment they press him, reach for a drawer, or get a clear look at his eyes, the thing behind them drops the act.

The fight. Mr. Betterton is the host; the Fluke rides him. Simple, not too hard; stat blocks in the bestiary. Two phases: put the undertaker down, and the Fluke tears free and leaps for a fresh head. A character it reaches saves or is taken. Kill the Fluke before it burrows, or before the taken PC turns on the party.

The Signature

With Betterton down, the morgue gives up what they came for. The autopsy ledger and the drawer tags carry one consulting physician across victim after victim, signed in the same neat hand: Dr. Aldous Pemberton.

Conclusion

Armed with verification that Dr. Pemberton was somehow involved, as well as his address, the players can now proceed to the Finale Scene.

pages.name: Stowe Away
pages.html:
Brasshold docks. Night. ~30-45 minutes.

The Stowe trail leads to Brasshold and the Maggie Mae, a harbor tug gone idle since the Blockade, her owner paid to take a long holiday. Stowe is aboard, hiding, and coming apart.

Brasshold's fishing docks are a graveyard since the Blockade, a long row of boats riding dead at their moorings in the fog. Only one shows any life. Down at the end a squat harbor tug, Maggie Mae flaking off her bow, has a lantern burning low in the wheelhouse and a shape moving behind the glass. A voice carries across the water before you are halfway down the boards, too high and too fast. "Who is that? Say who you are or keep walking. I mean it, I have a gun."

Once they name themselves, Stowe places the party as the help he has been praying for and waves them aboard. He is out of time, and he knows it.

Dead Water

Stowe is barely holding together and wants gone this minute. The party is not aboard a minute before boots sound in the fog: the Special Police have come for him.

The escape. Three jobs get the Maggie Mae underway: (1) start the engine, and throw off the (2) bow and the (3) stern lines. Stowe manages one a round on his own, so left to him she is clear in three; the party can take jobs to go faster, or leave them to him and cover the deck. Each job is one character's action and requires an appropriate skill check.

Every round the Special Police work the dock with gunfire and grappling hooks. A grapple left in place prevents the boat from casting off until the hook is cut. Cutting a grapple is an action, same as a job.

When all three jobs are done and no grapple holds her, the Maggie Mae swings out into the dark and the Police are left cursing on the boards. If Stowe goes down the jobs stall until someone gets him up or takes the wheel. Straight human fight, stat blocks in the bestiary, no Mythos here.

The Man Who Came Asking

The city falls away behind you, its few lit windows smearing in the fog, and the tug's engine settles into a slow heartbeat. Stowe stands at the wheel with both hands locked white on the spokes, and when he finally speaks his salesman's voice is gone.

Stowe is out of safe houses and out of nerve, and he begs the party to help him disappear:

"Weeks ago a soft-spoken doctor named Pemberton came to me and asked for money to help acquire certain old pages. That is how I first learned the pages existed, and I have thought of nothing since. Pemberton works in the sanitorium, but for the past few weeks my solicitor has been hounded by the Special Police. Luckily, I have been otherwise occupied and they have not yet had an opportunity to question me," he says.

"I have a dozen houses and I cannot sleep in any of them. I have paid every man I know, and it's useless. There is a thing coming for me, and money will not stop it. But, perhaps money can buy someone who can. Are you for hire?"

pages.name: Finale
pages.html:
Brownstone Lane, 30-45 minutes.

The home you approach could have been any on the block, walls made of brown-stone bricks and orange clay shingles. A turret on the left side of the house is likely a stairwell. The door is painted a dark green. Yet, even though it looks much like the other houses on the street, this one feels different. Whatever the opposite of 'curb appeal' is called, this house has it.

The door has been broken open and will not fully close. The Special Police have been through every room. Drawers dumped, furniture on its back, ten years of a careful life thrown across the floors. Pemberton is gone, and so is anything that mattered; the Police carried it off. What is left tells two stories and hides a third.

The housekeeper. In the back hall, blood, a dropped tea-tray, and a long drag-mark to the door with no body at the end of it. She was in the way when they came for the doctor, and they took her out with everything else.

The Study

The circle in the study. Chalked across the study floor, a summoning circle, a pentagram, black candles, the whole theatre of a rite. It is a fake, staged by the Special Police to paper over a warrantless seizure. The sigils are wrong, the chalk is fresh, and boot-scuffs cross the lines. An occult or investigative eye reads it as a plant in a moment.

Worth taking. The rooms hold nothing that moves the case, but a careful search turns up a consumable or two the Police missed. The party finds 1d3, rolled on the table.

d6 Consumable
1 Vial of Dr. Boonsboro's Nervine. Bonus action to end the Frightened condition on yourself.
2 A sealed spell scroll (roll on the scroll table).
3 Tincture of laudanum. Heals 2d4+2, then Poisoned for one hour.
4 Smelling salts. Action to end Stunned or Incapacitated on a creature you touch.
5 A sealed spell scroll (roll on the scroll table).
6 Flask of high-proof spirit. Thrown incendiary (2d6 fire).

What Was Left Behind

Behind a secret door (DC12 Investigation) in the basement, the characters can find the Shadow of Dr. Pemberton's study. The Police never found this door.

The door gives onto a low room that was meant to be forgotten. Something fills the far corner, a wet heaving mass the size of two men, and as your light touches it the faces open. Dozens of mouths set in stolen faces you half know, all speaking at once in the voices of the dead, and every one of them is smiling.

Seeing What Was Left Behind for the first time is a Mythos exposure. Each character makes a DC 17 Mythos check; on a failure, the character is Stunned until the start of its second turn as the players see something that should not exist. The creature is an Epic Boss and the repository of the Shadow's knowledge.

Rewards

If the party defeats the creature, they will find several preserved jars of brain matter, a page of the Pale Journals, and the Shadow's Journal, which tells who the Shadow is and what he has been doing.

and the less said of the Lady Ridgely's hat, the kinder we shall all be. But the parlours have lately been busy with a better puzzle than millinery. Where, the whole season should like to know, has Sir Reginald Stowe got to? Our newest gentleman, whose fortune still smells faintly of the foundry and whose title is not yet a year old, was to be the very ornament of Lord Preston's ball at Crown Ring, and sent not so much as a card of regret. He has not been seen at his club, nor at the opera, nor at any of the three suppers that would cheerfully have killed to seat him. A man may tire of society, your faithful Latchkey supposes. But a man who spent so freely to be let into it does not, as a rule, tire of it inside a fortnight and simply vanish.

pages.name: A NIGHT AT CROWN RING
pages.html:
By Honoria Easton, The Lantern

There is a war on, or so the broadsheets keep insisting, but you would not have credited it at Crown Ring on Saturday last, where Lord Preston threw open his doors and half the city's better money came dressed in what the blockade has left them.

The estate wore its finest. Every lamp in the long gallery was lit, hang the shortages, and the orchestra played until the small hours as though the dragons over the harbor were a rumor got up by the newspapers to spoil trade. There was sparkling wine, the real thing, run in past the warships at a price no one had the vulgarity to name aloud. The younger Miss Bowie wore green and danced with three lieutenants and a captain who ought to have known better. Old Lady Salisbury held court by the fire and told anyone who paused of the season she came out, which was, by her own arithmetic, during a different war.

It was beautiful, and it was a little obscene, and both were true at once. Outside the walls, the guns. Inside, the fiddles. Down in the lower wards this week they are burying people no orchestra will play for. But that is not, one supposes, what a ball is for.

Lord Preston made his toast to the city, to trade, and to better days. There is no crown in Anchester and no king to drink to; the only royalty this city ever minted is the kind you can spend, and the room drank to that with great feeling before going back to dancing.

pages.name: THE SILVER VOICE
pages.html:
By Constance Sharp, The Lantern

I met Vellora Sigh only once, at a small gathering in a quaint little parlour where the members of a literary society had come together to discuss words both old and new. I had gone as a skeptic, notebook in hand, expecting to leave with a column making fools of the whole solemn business. I left with none of that, and I have not stopped thinking of her since.

While the others were upstairs about their reading, she found a quiet corner and a second glass of wine for a young reporter she owed nothing, and we talked of the theatre for the better part of an hour. The great roles of her prime and the smaller ones she had loved better. The houses she had played and the sorry state of them now. She was generous about the work I had been too young to see, and kinder still about the little I had. She asked after my own people and listened to the answers as though they mattered, which a woman of her fame had no earthly reason to do. When at last I coaxed her, she gave me one line of Yoricina's mad scene from Small Town Murders, softly, just for me, in that low silver voice the critics could never quite describe, and the hair stood up on my arms.

She put me in mind of my own aunt, who is younger than Vellora was and has not a tenth of her spark, and whom I have let far too many weeks go by without a visit. That was Vellora's gift, on the boards and off them: she could make you forget, for an hour, why you had come, and be glad you had.

Now that great star of stage is gone, found in her rooms with the door locked from within, nothing taken and nothing disturbed, the cause of death set down as unascertained. I have read that word a great many times this season. I am told there is no more to say.

I do not believe there is no more to say. I believe there is a great deal more, and that someone has decided we are not to hear it. But Vellora would forgive me for not making this the column that says it. She would sooner be remembered for the silver in her voice than for the manner of its silencing.

So. She was kind to a reporter who had come to mock her. She was funnier than the rest of us together. And the city is quieter now in a way I do not like.

Rest, Madame. The house is dark, and the seats are full.

pages.name: WONDERS AT THE TOWER
pages.html:
By Silas Denton, The Lantern

It has been moored at the Tower for months now, and the crowds have not thinned.

The Carnival of Wandering Wonders came down out of the black between the stars some while ago, the only thing to slip past the blockade in a year, and has since settled across the yards below into the strangest few acres in Anchester. I went again on a wet evening expecting, by now, to be bored of the thing. I found instead a menagerie of creatures that have no business drawing breath in our air, a raven-winged young man who snuffs the lamps with a gesture and fills the dark with shapes that are not there, and a woman who sells you a cup of something hot and will not say what is in it. The crowds are still enormous. For the price of a ticket you may forget, for an hour, the guns over the harbor, and forgetting is the one luxury the siege has left us cheap.

The Baron who runs the show is everywhere and nowhere, all teeth and courtesy. But it is Madame Sixpence the queues form for, a fortune-wife whose readings have a way of coming true, and who told the man ahead of me, unasked, to go straight home to his children. He went white, and he went.

Stranger still is the company the wonders keep. Among the clerks and the sweethearts I marked more than a few sober gentlemen of medicine, and one or two with the grey pallor of the Sanitorium about them, come down to stand a long while before the cages and say nothing at all. What a doctor wants with a beast out of the far dark I could not tell you. But they keep coming. So, I confess, do I.

pages.name: Father Mercer Penance, thirty years the poor quarter's...
pages.html:
Father Mercer Penance, thirty years the poor quarter's priest, is dead. His Church calls the death sudden and natural, and will say nothing further.

By Constance Sharp

They are calling it a natural death, and perhaps it was. I met Father Mercer Penance only once, and briefly, at an evening's gathering of literary enthusiasts not a fortnight past, where old books and new words were the whole of the talk. He seemed to me a hale man, and a kind one.

He gave thirty years to the Martyr's quarter, the streets the rest of the city prefers not to name. By every account there, he knew each child in the ladle line by name, buried the paupers no one claimed, and fed the ones no one wanted, and never once suggested the poor had earned their poverty. The grief on those streets today is real, and loud, and everywhere.

He was not, they say, an easy man for his order to keep. He took seriously the questions his brothers found unbecoming, and he turned no frightened soul from his door for the strangeness of its fear. Our words that evening were few. He answered one question of mine kindly, declined another, and asked me, quietly, to be careful. I did not understand him then. I am beginning to.

He was found in his vestry, the door fast from the inside, and there the plain account ends. The Church gives out that the death was sudden and natural, and asks that it be mourned rather than examined. No cause has been named. No coroner has spoken. The inquiry has been taken up by officers who answer to no ward of this city.

I will honor the request to mourn him. I decline the request to stop asking.

pages.name: Who Feeds them Now?
pages.html:
Who Feeds them Now?

By Ezra Hebron

The line at the Martyr's Table formed this morning as it forms every morning, and this morning, for the first time in thirty years, Father Penance was not at the head of it. The copper still steamed. The bread was still cut. The children still came. That the door opened at all is the work of the men he trained to open it.

Chief among them is Brother Cobbe, a lay brother of the Church of the Martyr who has ladled soup in Brasshold since before most of its children were born. He was at his place before dawn, red-eyed and steady. "The Father would not have us close for grief," he said, wiping down a table that did not need wiping. "He fed them yesterday. We will feed them today. That is the whole of it."

It is not, in truth, the whole of it. The Table has always run close to empty, kept going on the Father's own purse and his gift for coaxing coin from comfortable pockets. Both are gone now. The lay brothers can carry the ladle. They cannot conjure what fills it.

The Church has asked this paper to say plainly what it will not say from the pulpit: that the Martyr's Table needs help, and needs it now. Tinned goods, bread, blankets, and coin may be left at the Rectory of the Martyr, where Canon Preston has undertaken to see that every gift reaches the Table and not the ledger.

There is a way to mourn a man that costs nothing and means little. There is another that keeps a poor child fed through a hard winter in his name. The Father, one suspects, would have had firm views on which the city ought to choose.

pages.name: The Collection Plate
pages.html:
The Collection Plate

Cheerful doings from the parishes, gathered by our man at the back of the nave

By Tabitha Chester

Grief is the city's fashion this week, and your correspondent will not argue with it. But the parishes go on about their small kindnesses, and a man may be forgiven for smiling at a few.

At the Provident Church's harvest bazaar, the Ladies' Aid raised a handsome sum, though not by the means intended. The tombola's grand prize, a fat goose donated by a farmer of tender heart, declined its part in the proceedings and led the curate a chase three times round the churchyard before being cornered in the font. Wagers on the outcome, your correspondent regrets to report, out-earned the raffle itself. The goose has since been pardoned and pensioned to the vicarage lawn, where it now bullies the verger.

The Martyr's orphans sang at the same event and did such damage to the hearts of the assembled that one dockman of enormous size and terrible reputation was seen to empty every pocket he owned into the collection plate, glare at anyone who dared notice, and depart at speed. The plate has not had such a night in living memory.

And this, which your correspondent sets down without a jest. When word went round of the appeal for the Martyr's Table, it was the poor quarter itself that gave first and gave most. A widow three weeks behind on her rent sent a tin of biscuits and a note that read, only, "For the little ones. He always found room for mine."

The comfortable parishes have some catching up to do.

pages.name: FOG OFF NORTH RIDGE
pages.html:
FOG OFF NORTH RIDGE

Marcus Aberdeen, Garrison Times

Three nights running, the watch on North Ridge has logged the same report: steamers west of the ridge, standing off the low ground the old maps mark Paschendale.

They do not close. They come in on the evening fog and stand out again on the dawn tide. In the hour between, a good glass counts more smoke than a man would like. The hulls are Sous Terreborgois. No argument there. Why an armada of that draught should trouble a stretch of drowned pasture no army has fought over in thirty years is a question the ridge has put to the war office and had no answer to.

This paper will say only what the chart says. Paschendale is flat, wet, and astride the last soft road inland the blockade has not shut. Ships do not hold that station for nothing. They are taking soundings.

The ridge would do well to keep its fuses dry and its returns current.

pages.name: THE MEN ON THE WALL
pages.html:
THE MEN ON THE WALL

Halbert Cambridge, Garrison Times

I spent Thursday night on the east wall with the third of the line, where the dragons come lowest and the guns can least reach them.

There is not much to tell, and that is the worst of it. The men stand to at dusk, watch the fog for shadows, and stand down at dawn having fired nothing. A boy named Galena showed me how he has taught himself to sleep upright with his eyes open. His sergeant, a hard old hand called Hancock, said the boy would unlearn the trick or be buried in it, and then gave him his own blanket for the cold.

Rations are short and getting shorter. The bread is a week stale and the tea is mostly not tea. No one complains where an officer can hear, and every man complains where I can. They are not afraid of the dragons any longer, which troubles me more than the dragons do.

They asked me to put their names in the paper, so someone at home would know they had stood the wall. I have not the column for all of them. I will carry the list instead.

ELKTON'S PATENT LIMBS For the soldier returned less than he went. Fitted and balanced. Terms for the pensioned.

SURGEON-MAJOR FRANE, WAR HERO, DEAD AT HIS DESK

Jeff Frederick, Garrison Times

Surgeon-Major Thurston Frane, Anchester Medical Corps, was found dead at his desk on Tuesday last. Fifty-one years, thirty in service.

Frane came up through three campaigns and finished his posting here, tending the officers invalided home to this quarter. Those who served under him report a steady hand, a short manner, and a man who never once went sick himself. The war office lists the cause as sudden and unexplained and directs that no further conclusion be drawn.

No family survives him. Among his charges was Major L. Wakes, Anchester lines, whose recovery Frane had taken as his own. Arrangements pending. The corps is short a good surgeon and will not soon replace him.
