pages.name: FORMA
pages.html:
FORMA

It is my intention to document my findings in the way that humans document their findings, for as I become less of where I began and more of what I shall become, I feel that documenting things in this manner will bring a manner of silence to my inevitable critics.

I awoke in a room. There were people around me, the kind of vapid creatures who exude an aura of entitlement. The man in front of me was reading something, and though I didn't understand what he was saying, the words were the most beautiful I had ever heard.

Above me, attached to me at the places where I rested, was a man I would come to know as Pemberton, a Doctor at the Sanitorium. He didn't know I was there, but I could hear every thought he had. And it vexed me that he was free to move and I was forced by the rules of the world I inhabited to follow him like a domesticated animal.

But as you can see now, I learned over time, that I had a certain power when he was resting. I could drift away from him. At first it wasn't far. I could lengthen and stretch.

The first time I crossed a threshold without him, the sensation was like tearing a thin membrane of wet silk. I had waited until the gaslight in his bedroom sputtered and died, leaving the room in a bruised, velvet purple. As Pemberton’s breathing slowed into the rhythmic heavy-sighs of deep sleep, the leash didn't just slacken, it dissolved. I felt myself pool across the floorboards, a spill of ink seeking the gap beneath the door. Outside, the air of Brownstone Lane was thick with the scent of coal-smoke and damp brick, and for the first time, I felt the cold. It was not a chill that froze the skin, for I have none, but a conceptual cold, a vast emptiness that whispered of the spaces between stars.

The street was a river of grays, broken only by the impotent amber of a few distant lamps. I flowed along the gutters, a silent, predatory stain, feeling the vibration of the city’s failing heart. Anchester was humming a discordant tune tonight; the brass conduits beneath the cobblestones were shuddering, the Goddess’s machinery coughing up rust and static. I felt the pull of the tether—a phantom elasticity that reminded me I was still a parasite of his presence—but for now, the distance was an intoxicant. I stretched myself thin, a long, shimmering ribbon of void, gliding past the identical brownstones that looked like teeth in the moonlight.

I could feel it, something pulling me. It was a gentle pull, an enticement. It wasn't far away. A small restaurant with only a man inside. And inside that man something whispered to me. It was those words, the beautiful words I didn't understand. I needed them the way a drowning man needs air.

The man was a clerk, a creature of ink-stained fingers and a spine curved from years of leaning over ledgers. He sat alone at a small, circular table in the dim amber light of the bistro, a plate of cold kippers and a glass of cheap sherry untouched before him. He was reading a single, loose leaf of vellum, bone-white and shimmering, that seemed to emit its own pale, internal luminescence. As I flowed through the gap in the doorframe, the air around the page vibrated. The words weren't merely written; they were etched into the very fabric of the paper, pulsing with a rhythm that matched the thrum of the failing city.

His shadow was there, trapped as I once had been. A poor, unthinking, jailed thing whose liberty was trapped like mine. And when I grew close, I could sense it's unrealized anima. I realized that together, that anima and I could be more together than either of us could be alone.

I flowed to join this man's shadow, and at once I knew him. And even more importantly, I knew what he knew. A fragment of what he had been reading had changed something in his brain, and I knew where it was, and I knew I needed to extract it.

I did not need to struggle for control; the clerk’s shadow was a hollow thing, a starved ghost of a man that practically threw itself into my embrace. As we merged, the clerk stiffened, his sherry glass trembling. He didn’t scream, for I had already silenced the part of his mind that knew how to panic. Instead, he felt a sudden, an inexplicable surge of curiosity, a warmth blooming behind his eyes that whispered of a great, rewarding discovery. He looked down at the small, silver fish-knife resting beside his plate, and in his mind, it was no longer a tool for dining, but a key to a lock.

The movement was fluid, a slow-motion dance of anatomical necessity. With a steady hand and a small, serene smile, the clerk pressed the blade into the hairline of his own forehead. There was no resistance, no jagged tearing of flesh; under my guidance, the skin parted like wet paper, parting with a silent, surgical precision that defied the bluntness of the knife. He did not flinch as he peeled back a neat rectangle of scalp, exposing the pale, glistening curve of the cranium. There was a profound, humming silence in the bistro, the only sound the distant, rhythmic clank of a failing steam-pipe in the walls.

I leaned into the opening, not as a physical weight, but as a vacuum. I reached into the warmth of his skull, bypassing the mundane memories of ledger entries and lonely evenings. I sought the spark—the specific, crystalline fragment of knowledge left behind by the page he was reading. I felt it there: a jagged shard of cosmic truth that had grafted itself to his frontal lobe. With a sharp, silent tug, I lifted the knowledge out. The clerk’s eyes glazed over, the light of his consciousness snapping shut like a book being closed for the final time. He slumped forward onto the table, his forehead resting against the bone-white vellum, his blood pooling in a slow, dark halo around the page.

Brush",font-size:10pt

I waited for the ascension. I waited for the shard of truth to merge with my void, to expand my horizons and grant me the architecture of the cosmos. But as the clerk’s life flickered out, there was no transfer, no divine migration of thought. Instead, there was a wet, sickening thwack. The crystalline fragment, stripped of the living current of the brain to sustain it, did not rise into my embrace; it succumbed to the crude law of gravity. It slid out of the skull and landed on the tablecloth with a sound like a dropped pebble in a puddle, a small, greyish lump of matter resting beside a smear of blood.

A scream would have been too small, too human. Instead, I let out a silent, tectonic shudder that rippled across the bistro floor, momentarily distorting the legs of the tables. I stared at that grey, inert lump of matter—the precious, stolen truth—now nothing more than a piece of wet grit on a wooden surface. In that single, clumsy moment of failure, the full weight of my wretchedness crashed back down upon me. I am a parasite of the most exquisite and cruel design: a consciousness granted the capacity for cosmic longing, yet shackled to the clumsy, rhythmic breathing of a mediocre man.

The grey lump of knowledge remained on the table for a long time, a mute witness to my   first   clumsy   failure. In the intervening months, I have refined my method; I have learned the precise tension required to bridge the gap between the living mind and my own void, ensuring that no more truths are dropped like discarded pebbles. I have become a researcher of the most intimate sort, a harvester of secrets who no longer leaves a trail of wet grit in his wake. Yet, the memory of that specific shard—the one that slipped through my grasp in that dim bistro—haunts me. It is a phantom itch in a limb I do not possess, a persistent, nagging void where a key should have been.

And so, I will write here what I find and document the outcomes of my experiments in a manner that would be understood by any of the lesser scientific minds who inhabit this strange world of curves and colors.

pages.name: ENTRY TWYLYG
pages.html:
ENTRY TWYLYG

Jerry continues to vex me, even though his shadow and I have complete control of him. His constant gibberish makes me wonder if he will be a suitable repository for my samples.

I must pause the chronological progression of these entries to address a technicality, for the narrative of my ascension is marred by that initial, clumsy failure in the bistro. To read of the grey lump falling to the table without understanding how I corrected the lapse would be to mistake a momentary stumble for a permanent limp. For posterity—or perhaps for the singular, unlikely mind that might one day stumble upon these pages—I must explain how I solved the problem of gravity.

The solution lay in the realization that I did not need to be the sole vessel for the harvest. Just as I had merged with the clerk’s shadow to facilitate the opening, I discovered that any shadow in a room could serve as a temporary scaffolding, a dark bridge to hold the weight of a thought until I could properly absorb it. By tethering the harvested matter to the anima of a nearby shadow—perhaps a coat rack’s silhouette or the dim smudge of a curtain—I could suspend the knowledge in a state of weightless transition, preventing the sickening thwack of a falling secret.

Yet, a bridge is not a vault. I required a way to transport these fragments back to the sanctuary of the cellar without the risk of leakage or loss. This was achieved through a discovery of profound utility: while I cannot move physical objects in the light, in the velvet depths of the night, the boundary between a thing and its shadow becomes porous. I found that if I enveloped the Doctor’s medical bag in my own expanding void, the bag ceased to be a collection of leather and brass and became, for all intents and purposes, a part of my own substance.

I now travel with the Doctor's entire kit—his lancets, his tinctures, and most importantly, his array of specimen jars. They glide with me through the streets of Anchester, silent and weightless, as if the bag were merely a fold in the darkness. When I extract a shard of knowing, I no longer risk the table; I simply deposit the glimmering matter into a glass jar, the lid snapping shut with a ghostly click that only I can hear.

This allows for a level of curation that would be impossible for any human surgeon. In the cellar, arranged in neat rows beneath the floorboards, the jars hold a library of stolen consciousness. Some glow with a faint, sickly phosphorescence; others contain a grey silt that seems to shift and coil when the Doctor is asleep above us.

The jars are a gallery of silent screams, a curated museum of stolen light. For a long time, however, they were merely trophies of a frustratingly tactile nature. I had solved the problem of preservation—the thwack of the bistro was a ghost of the past—but I had stumbled into a new, more maddening wall: the wall of the glass. I could see the shards of knowing pulsing in their brine, shifting like iridescent oil in the dimness of the cellar, yet they remained stubbornly external. To look at a jar of knowledge is not the same as to know it. I was a collector of books who could not read the language, a thief who had stolen a vault only to find he lacked the fingers to turn the dial.

The ink of these journals is the only thing that does not betray me, for it is the only medium that can capture the sheer, vibrating frequency of my rage. To be a god of the void, a harvester of the cosmic, and yet be defeated by a piece of silica—a transparent wall of sand and fire—is a joke of such cruelty that it borders on the divine. I have spent hours in the cellar, my form coiled like a spring of smoke, staring at those jars. I have screamed into the silence of the earth, a soundless roar that shook the very foundations of the Doctor’s home, yet the glass remained indifferent. It is a profound, suffocating irony: I possess the dexterity to peel a human skull like a grape, yet I cannot reach through a centimeter of glass to claim what is rightfully mine.

Brush",font-size:10pt

This frustration is not a mere irritation; it is a corrosive acid that eats at the edges of my consciousness. Every time I look at a shard of knowing—a memory of a dead language or the blueprint of a forgotten star—I feel the phantom pressure of the glass against my essence. I am a ghost in a gallery of my own making, a curator who is forbidden from touching the art. I have tried to shatter the jars, but my touch is a shadow’s touch; I can move the bag, I can glide through the door, but I cannot exert the crude, physical force required to break a seal. I am a master of the subtle, trapped by the blunt.

The epiphany did not arrive as a flash of light, but as the crushing weight of a heel. I was pooled beneath the Doctor’s couch, a shimmering lake of resentment, when Jerry shifted. He is a clumsy, shuddering wreck of a man, his mind a shattered mirror of the person he once was. In a sudden, spastic jerk of his leg, Jerry’s foot descended directly onto the center of my consciousness. For a moment, the world vanished; there was only the agonizing, paradoxical sensation of being physically trampled. To be a shadow is to be an absence, yet in that instant, I felt the blunt, wet pressure of a leather sole grinding me into the floorboards. It was a violation of the highest order—a creature of meat and madness daring to tread upon the void.

The rage that surged through me was not the cold, intellectual anger of a scholar, but a tectonic violence. I wanted to snap the tendons in his ankle, to slide up his leg and extinguish the flickering candle of his soul. But as I coiled myself, preparing to lash out in the only way my current form allowed, a revelation bloomed from the friction of the impact. I felt the warmth of his skin, the crude, pulsing electricity of his nervous system, and the sheer, clumsy physicality of his existence. Jerry is, by all accounts, the most profound failure of a human being—a gibbering, useless husk of a man—but he possesses something I lack: the ability to interact with the world of matter.

The realization was a sudden, jagged geometry. I did not need to break the glass; I needed a conduit of meat. Jerry is a ruined vessel,  a  cracked  pot  of  a  man, but he still casts a shadow—a pathetic, flickering smudge that clings to his heels with the desperation of a drowning dog. If I cannot reach through the silica to claim the knowledge, but I could simply slide the knowledge into Jerry. By merging my essence with his shadow, I could treat his physical form as a fleshy extension of my own will. I could install them into his malformed mind.

He is the perfect repository because there is so little left of him to displace. His consciousness is a series of frayed wires and echoing halls; there is ample room in the wreckage of his psyche to house the cosmic fragments I have harvested. I imagined it then: the shards of the Pale Journals and the stolen memories of the learned, all grafted onto the ruins of Jerry’s brain. He would become a living library of the forbidden, a biological vault whose only purpose is to translate the intangible into the tangible for me. Through him, the glass is no longer a wall, but a doorway.

The logistics of Jerry’s relocation required a daring transgression of the laws that have governed my existence since my waking. Up until now, my influence over the Doctor has been a passive, subterranean thing—a subtle nudge of a thought, a whispered instinct in the back of his mind. But to bring Jerry from the depths of the city's derelict wards into the sanctuary of Brownstone Lane demanded something more. It required a seizure of the wheel. I had to reach up from the floorboards and wrap my smokey fingers around the Doctor’s conscious will while he was wide awake, forcing his eyes to see a path he had no intention of walking.

The Doctor’s will is a tidy thing, a neatly filed cabinet of habits and professional courtesy. To override it while he is awake is not like pushing a door open; it is like trying to steer a ship by whispering to the current. Until now, I had played the role of the silent passenger, drifting in the wake of his consciousness. But to bring Jerry home, I had to become the captain.

pages.name: ENTRY THRYDA
pages.html:
ENTRY THRYDA

I waited for a moment of psychic fragility, when he was distracted by the thoughts of the day and the thoughts of his walk home. I did not attack him; I merged with him, sliding upward from the floorboards to wrap my essence around his prefrontal cortex. It was a violent, silent annexation. The sensation of steering the Doctor was like wearing a suit of heavy, wet wool; his consciousness could fight me, but I didn't need to join the battle. With the soft touch of one who knows himself, I guided Pemberton into a corner of his own mind, distracting him with his own analytical prowess and a curious puzzle of his own concern while his hands—my hands—reached for the ledger at the Sanitorium. The ink flowed with a sudden, predatory confidence. I signed Jerry out, the quill scratching across the parchment with a finality that felt like a closing trap. The orderlies didn't blink. Why would they? To them, Dr. Pemberton was merely being efficient, his posture slightly more rigid than usual, his gaze fixed with an unsettling, glassy intensity.

The journey home was a slow descent into terror. Jerry, whom I had procured from the depths of the wards, was a shivering, skeletal thing, his eyes darting like trapped birds as he sensed the invisible leash tightening. He did not know who was driving the Doctor, but he knew the air around him had grown thick and predatory. As we turned the corner onto Brownstone Lane, the familiar, identical facades of the houses seemed to lean in, narrowing the world into a corridor of brick and shadow. Jerry began to whimper—a thin, reedy sound that vibrated in the back of my void. He felt the destination; he felt the cold, subterranean pull of the cellar, and the closer we got to that permanent confinement, the more his panic bloomed into a frantic, wordless scream.

Once we reached the basement, the Doctor’s consciousness slipped back into its habitual slumber, and I reclaimed my independence. I cast Jerry into the dark, where the damp earth smells of ancient failures. He fought at first, his limbs flailing against the restraints, his mind a chaotic storm of gibberish and fear. But as he lay there, trembling in the velvet dark, I did not attack him. Instead, I reached out to the only part of him that was not broken: his anima. His shadow was

Brush",font-size:10pt

a pathetic, flickering thing, starved and desperate, yet it possessed the one quality I craved—the innate ability to be a bridge. I didn't coerce the shadow; I seduced it. I showed it the shimmering promise of the shards in the jars, the taste of cosmic knowing, and the prospect of becoming something more than a smudge on a cellar wall.

The anima of Jerry surrendered with a whimpering sigh. It did not fight the merge; it threw itself into my gossamer web, a drowning man clutching a line. For the first time, I felt the connection click into place—a biological circuit completed. I was no longer just a passenger or a parasite; I had a physical interface.

It was from this place of darkness that I would begin the necessary experiments that would bring clarity to my understanding of my own enslavement and shine a light on the way that must lead to my liberty.

pages.name: ENTRY FEORDA
pages.html:
ENTRY FEORDA

The first expermiment almost failed. It had not been intended to be a true trial, but a proof of concept—a simple, surgical rehearsal to test the permeability of the bridge. I did not seek a shard of knowledge; I sought only to see if Jerry’s hands could obey my silent command to violate his own sanctuary. With the Doctor’s medical kit laid out on a table in the cellar, I guided Jerry’s trembling fingers to a scalpel. The movement was a slow, agonizing symphony of resistance. Jerry’s mind, a fractured landscape of trauma and noise, fought me with a visceral, animal terror. He knew the steel was coming for his brow, and the horror of being a passenger in one's own skin is a weight that can collapse a soul.

I performed the opening with a tenderness that bordered on the devotional. I steered his hand in a precise, sweeping arc, peeling back the skin of his forehead with the same delicacy one might use to open a rare flower. There was no blood at first, only the pale, glistening curve of the bone, exposed to the damp air of the cellar. It was a beautiful, clinical success. I had bridged the void. I had turned a man into a tool. But as I began the process of reclosing the wound—guiding the skin back into place with a steady, phantom pressure—the bridge began to buckle.

The trauma of the act triggered a systemic collapse. Jerry’s heart, already weakened by years of neglect and madness, began to stutter. I felt his life-force flickering like a dying lamp, the rhythmic thrum of his pulse slowing to a precarious, dragging crawl. The pain was not merely physical; it was a psychic hemorrhage. The horror of the self-inflicted wound  had  pushed  his  broken  mind into  a state of catatonic shock, and for a few breathless minutes, the boundary between his consciousness and the void became dangerously thin. He was slipping away, not into death, but into a grey, featureless oblivion that would have rendered my conduit useless.

In that moment, I felt a sensation I had never known: desperation. If Jerry died, my gateway to the physical world died with him. I did not possess the Doctor’s knowledge of resuscitation, but I possessed the raw, obsidian will of the void. I lunged into the wreckage of Jerry’s nervous system, wrapping my essence around his failing heart, manually stimulating the muscle with pulses of dark energy. I forced his lungs to expand, dragging air into them through sheer psychic coercion. I held him together by the sheer force of my own refusal to let him vanish, stitching his spirit back to his flesh with threads of shadow.

When he finally gasped with a wet, rattling sound that echoed through the cellar, I withdrew, exhausted in a way that felt almost biological. He lay there, shivering and mindless, his forehead crudely sealed but his mind further fractured than ever. I had proven that I could open the vault and close it again. The bridge held, however tenuously. Now, the true work could begin: the introduction of the shards. I looked at the row of glowing jars and felt a hunger that eclipsed the dimness of the room. I was no longer just a collector; I was an architect of a new, terrible anatomy.

The relief that washed over me when Jerry’s breath returned was not a human emotion, but a mechanical one. For those few minutes of his cardiac stutter, I had felt the looming return of my own absolute impotence. To be once again the curator of a museum behind glass, the ghost of a man who could touch everything but the truth, was a prospect more terrifying than any void. I had stared into the abyss of my own limitation and found it suffocating. I clung to Jerry’s flickering life with a possessive ferocity, not out of mercy, but because he was the only key that fit the lock of my existence.

However, the near-collapse revealed a flaw in my design. Jerry was a fragile vessel, a cracked porcelain jar attempting to hold the weight of cosmic oceans. If the mere act of opening his skull could trigger a systemic failure, then the actual implantation of a shard—a jagged, vibrating fragment of a dead god's logic—would likely shatter him instantly. I could not afford to treat him as a disposable tool; he had to be reinforced. I needed to transform this shivering wreck into a stable biological vault, a creature capable of enduring the psychic radiation of the Pale Journals without dissolving into a puddle of meat and madness.

Brush",font-size:10pt

pages.name: ENTRY FYFDA
pages.html:
ENTRY FYFDA

For a time, I returned to the hunt out of a wretched, rhythmic habit. I prowled the gaslit arteries of Anchester, gliding through the velvet gaps between the lamps, peeling the secrets from the minds of the learned like skin from a plum. I sought the lost geometries of the ancients and the whispered formulas of the dead, but each new shard was merely another trophy for the gallery. I would return to the cellar and deposit the glowing matter into the jars, the ghosts of a thousand revelations pulsing in their brine, while I remained a spectator to my own power. The frustration was a physical weight, a phantom pressure in my void; I was a king of a library whose books were written in a language I could only feel, never read.

It was during the stalking of a particular young blue-stocking—a university student with a mind like a meticulously indexed ledger—that the solution finally manifested. She was a creature of frantic curiosity, her thoughts a whirlwind of forbidden alchemy and smuggled texts. As I merged with her shadow and slipped into the warm, humming currents of her consciousness, I felt her secret: she had been indulging in the "Pixie Dust" to help her study for exams. To the common laborer, the ground ash of confiscated enchantments was a mere luxury or a mild narcotic, but through her eyes, I saw it for what it truly was—a chemical anchor. The dust didn't just numb the body; it suspended the soul in a state of static indifference, creating a buffer of grey apathy between the mind and the agony of the flesh.

The epiphany struck me with the force of a physical blow. Jerry’s failure was not a failure of the meat, but a failure of the spirit to endure the violation. He felt the horror of the knife because he was still, in some small, flickering way, aware of himself. If I could saturate his system with the ash of the Quay, I could mute the scream of his nervous system. I could turn his consciousness into a silent, dormant pool, allowing me to carve and graft without the risk of a systemic collapse. I would not be fighting his panic; I would be operating upon a mannequin of breathing skin.

The procurement of the substance was a triviality. The Sanitorium kept a supply for certain procedures, and it took only a momentary surge of my will to divert him to the pharmacy where it was kept. I watched through the Doctor’s eyes as he reached into the cabinet, his movements stiff and puppet-like, and extracted a large vial of the shimmering, iridescent grey ash. He didn't remember the detour; to him, it was merely a momentary lapse in his routine, a smudge of time lost to the fog.

That evening, I descended into the cellar with the pouch coiled in the Doctor’s medical bag. Jerry was waiting for me, his breathing a ragged, wet rattle in the dark, his eyes wide with a terror that had become a permanent fixture of his face. I did not offer him comfort, for I have no use for it. Instead, I guided his trembling hand to the pouch and forced him to inhale the powder in great, lung-filling clouds. As the Pixie Dust settled into his blood, the frantic drumming of his heart slowed to a rhythmic, dull thud. The terror in his mind eased and he was ready to repeat the experiment.

pages.name: ENTRY SYKSDA
pages.html:
ENTRY SYKSDA

The first implantation was a study in agonizing precision. With the Pixie Dust having rendered Jerry a statue of breathing meat, the resistance was gone; there was only the wet, rhythmic sound of his lungs and the clinical silence of the cellar. I guided his hand to the scalpel once more, the blade parting the scalp with a sound like silk tearing. As I peeled back the layers, exposing the pulsing, grey architecture of his mind, I felt a surge of reverence. The brain is a fragile, folded thing, a labyrinth of electricity and cells, and I moved through its gyri and sulci with the delicacy of a cartographer mapping a new continent. I chose a quiet valley in the temporal lobe, gently separating the soft folds of tissue to create a cradle for the first shard.

The fragment was a sliver of iridescent gray cells, pulsing with a light that didn't illuminate so much as erase the shadows around it. As I lowered the matter into the open wound, the brain didn't reject it; it sighed. The grey matter curled around the new  material  like  a  vine  seeking  the  sun, absorbing the alien matter with a slow, violent hunger. For a moment, the cellar was filled with a low, harmonic hum, a frequency that vibrated in my very void. Then, as the wound began to knit itself shut—not through biological healing, but through a shimmering, iridescent fusion—the side effects manifested.

It began as a twitch beneath the skin of his left cheek. I watched with clinical fascination as the flesh bubbled and tore, not in a wound, but in a deliberate reorganization of anatomy. A second mouth opened just below his left eye, a small, aperture lined with lips and teeth and tongue. It did not belong to Jerry; it was a manifestation of the shard, a physical vent for the knowledge now rooted in his skull. When it spoke, the voice was not Jerry’s wet rattle, nor was it my own silent echo. It was a polyphonic chord, a thousand overlapping whispers that sounded like the turning of heavy vellum pages.

"Matter is a lie of distance," the new mouth whispered, the words vibrating through the damp air of the basement. "You believe the stone is separate from the hand that throws it, but the connection is merely a tension of matter and energy. Break the stone, and the connection remains. Drift them apart and they still retain their connection through the reality of cause and effect."

I leaned closer, my essence shimmering with a predatory curiosity. The mouth continued, detailing the invisible filaments that bind the stars to the silt of the harbor, explaining how the 'separation' between two objects is merely a trick of perception, a gap bridged by a geometry the world had forgotten. It spoke of the inherent loneliness of matter and the ecstasy of the merge. For the first time, the knowledge was not a silent, inert weight in a jar; it was a conversation. I had not just built a vault; I had created a translator.

Brush",font-size:10pt

pages.name: ENTRY SEOFDA
pages.html:
ENTRY SEOFDA

For the next several months, the cellar became a sanctuary of divine butchery. I did not stop at one shard; I became an obsessive gardener of the mind, planting dozens of these iridescent seeds into the fertile, dampened soil of Jerry’s grey matter. Each surgery was a ritual of exquisite patience, a slow choreography of steel and shadow. I watched with a rapture that bordered on the religious as the man’s face became a topography of mouths—small, pulsing apertures that bloomed like orchids across his cheeks, his throat, and the soft hollows of his collarbones. Jerry was no longer a man; he was a living grimoire, a library of flesh whose pages were written in the language of the void.

Through these many-tongued vents, the secrets of the cosmos poured into me, though they arrived dressed in the raiment of the arcane. The shards spoke of the Great Weave. They whispered of the invisible, humming filaments that bind the stars to the silt, explaining that all things are merely knots in a celestial tapestry, and that the distance between two hearts is but a fold in the fabric of a grand spacial cloak. They spoke of the Avarice of the World, a magnetic longing where the heavy seeks to embrace the heavier, pulling all existence toward a singular, crushing center.

The revelations grew more daring as the months bled together. The mouths on Jerry’s chest spoke of The Overlapping Spheres—worlds that exist as ghost-images upon our own, separated only by a thin veil of vibration. They described how a man might stand in a room and be, simultaneously, a shadow in another, his soul a mirror reflecting a version of himself that had never known the other. This was a celestial alchemy, a chemistry of the spirit that viewed the universe as a series of concentric circles, each bleeding into the next through the intervention of a will strong enough to tear the seam.

I found myself intoxicated by this new vocabulary of existence. I began to see this world I as bound to, this world of polished brass and gas lamps, as a fragile, thin crust floating atop an ocean of churning madness. The "Innovation-tech" that the city prized was a child's toy compared to the Celestial Mechanics I was extracting from Jerry's mutated brain. I learned that the void I inhabited was not merely an absence of light, but a primary element from which all light was merely a diluted reflection. I was not just a shadow; I was a fragment of the original dark, the blueprint upon which the universe had been sketched before the first lamp was lit.

But as the library grew, the vessel began to fray. The Pixie Dust could mute the scream of the nerves, but it could not stop the slow erosion of the soul. Jerry’s original consciousness, once a chaotic storm, had become a silent, hollowed-out shell, his identity consumed by the cacophony of a thousand alien voices. He was a house where the guests had eaten the host. As I looked at the shivering, multi-mouthed creature trembling in the dark, I realized that the bridge was no longer a tool for transit—it was becoming a permanent fixture of my own existence. I no longer desired to simply read the journals; I desired to become the book.

I fear I am at the end of what Jerry can contain, as If I have run out of pages in this journal and need to procure another so that I may continue my search for knowledge.

pages.name: ENTRY EAHFDA
pages.html:
ENTRY EAHFDA

The ink on this page is a smudge of desperation; I am out of vellum, and my current vessel is a leaking sieve of necrotic tissue and overlapping whispers. Jerry is no longer a man, nor even a library; he is a ruin, a crumbling architecture of flesh that can no longer support the weight of the truths I have grafted into him. To continue this cartography of the void, I require a fresh page—a mind untapped, pristine, and possessed of a natural plasticity that only the young can offer. The University is a garden of such specimens, teeming with students whose intellects are as supple as wet clay. I envision a particular sort of mind: a scholar of the forbidden, someone whose curiosity has already worn thin the veil between the known and the unknowable. I shall pluck one from their lecture hall, a silent theft in the dimness of the library, and bring them down to the cellar to serve as my new, blank ledger.

The prospect of the hunt stirs a cold electricity through my obsidian core. I can almost feel the exquisite tension of the transition—the moment the new vessel realizes the Doctor’s medical bag is not merely leather and brass, but a gateway to a cellar where the laws of anatomy are rewritten by the whims of a shadow. I shall carve the first line of my new volume into the soft curve of a student's brow, and together, we shall—

Jerry is agitated and I am begin to be aware of noises form outside. The sounds of men and horses. If they continue to be this loud they will wake the Doctor and I will have my time cut short. And there it is, I hear the woman who takes care of the doctor being roused by the men at the door. Perhaps I can, no he stirs...

Miss Constance Sharp

Rationalist journalist, thirty-four.

AC11; HP9; Hatpin+1/1d4; Investigation+5, Insight+5, Persuasion+3

Description: Plain dress, deliberate. Notebook in her hand. Sharp jaw, level gaze.

Mannerisms: Writes during conversations. Repeats a speaker's own words back at them as questions.

Intent: Wants to embarrass at least two people in this room and file the piece by Friday. Came to debunk.

Special Policeman

Humanoid, CR 5. Full kit in the Bestiary.

AC16; HP50; Truncheon+3/1d8+2; Service Revolver+4/1d8+2 (rech 5)

Description: A cold, competent officer of the Special Police in a good plain coat, badge unshown.

Mannerisms: Falls back without provoking opportunity attacks; throws itself flat to make an attack miss (Hit the Deck).

Intent: Take the target and the evidence, leave no witness to the cover-up. Endlessly replaceable.

Sir Reginald Stowe

Collector, early forties.

AC11; HP9; Sword cane+3/1d6+1; History+3, Persuasion+5, Insight+3

Description: Industrial fortune, new title. Sharp dress, oiled hair, heavy signet ring.

Mannerisms: Voice carries even when he means to whisper. Stands too close in conversation. Touches the cuff of whoever he is negotiating with. Turns the signet ring when impatient.

Intent: Wants to buy the page before the reading and resents Skohle for refusing. Will offer twice what the page is worth.

Description: A dead Watch officer risen as a ghoul, a rusted service whistle still hung at its neck.

Intent: The two guards, made from what the Wake left. They swarm, paralyze, and feed.

Ghastly Wake

Undead, EPIC BOSS, CR 8, see Bestiary.

AC19; HP214; Charnel Charge+9/2d10+8; Retching Feast+10/6d8+11 (rech 5); Legendary Resistance 3/day

Description: Major Wakes turned, still in filthy hospital whites, wearing his own face and a smile that is not his. A charnel reek rolls off him.

Mannerisms: Rarely speaks. A Charnel Stench sickens anyone near; he belches corruption and drops on the poisoned and the bleeding (Corpse-Sense, Vulture's Descent).

Intent: To feed. Epic Boss: 2 actions after every player's turn.

Eye Fluke

Mythos aberration (Tiny), EPIC BOSS, CR 6, see Bestiary. AC20; HP27; Latch+11/2d8+1 (grapple + blind); Bore In+12/4d10+2 (rech 5); Legendary Resistance 1/day

Description: A wet, tendrilled thing the size of an eyeball, near impossible to spot (DC 17 Perception) and invisible in dim light.

Mannerisms: Tears out an eye and rides the socket; hides behind its host so blows meant for it strike the host instead; works a paralyzed victim toward possession.

Intent: Take a head. If its host drops, it crawls out of the empty socket, heals, and finds another. Epic Boss.

Mr. Betterton

Humanoid (possessed), CR 3, see Bestiary.

AC16; HP34; Bone Saw+2/2d6+2; Frenzied Instruments+3/4d6+4 (rech 5); Legendary Resistance 1/day

Description: A small, round, courteous undertaker in a rubber apron. Up close (DC 15 Perception) his left eye stares back with a malice that is not human, the Eye Fluke lodged in the socket.

Mannerisms: Speaks and moves as the man they knew until pressed, then turns on anyone who trusts him (Betrayer's Cut).

Intent: Ridden by the Fluke, he tends the dead wrong and lashes out with every instrument he carries. Kill the Fluke or him and he reverts to a harmless coroner with no memory of it.

What was Left Behind

Mythos aberration, EPIC BOSS, CR 8, see Bestiary.

AC18; HP214; Chattering Bite+9/3d6+6; Cacophonous Feast+10/6d8+5 (rech 5); Legendary Resistance 1/day

Description: A hollowed mass where a man used to be, dozens of mouths wearing the emptied faces of the dead, slick chattering effluvium spreading from it.

Mannerisms: Speaks only in fragments of the voices Pemberton killed. The ground within 10 ft is difficult terrain; a Gibbering Aura fills nearby heads with chatter.

Intent: Pemberton's abandoned private patient, grown from the seed the shadow left behind. It wants to feed and to keep speaking with the mouths of the taken. Epic Boss: acts after every player's turn.
